answerBody:
The final rule should make federal preemption the governing default once a local rights-of-way approval exceeds a clear shot clock or demands fees beyond a cost-based ceiling, subject to a narrow local rebuttal for incomplete applications, applicant-caused delay, or documented public-safety conflicts. That default is more faithful to the Communications Act and better suited to broadband deployment than preserving local control until each carrier proves that a particular ordinance, invoice, or practice blocks service.

Section 253(a) of the Communications Act bars any state or local legal requirement that prohibits, or has the effect of prohibiting, telecommunications service. Section 253(c) preserves local authority to manage public rights-of-way and obtain fair, reasonable, publicly disclosed, competitively neutral compensation. Read together, local governments keep operational control over traffic, restoration, safety, coordination, and real cost recovery, but not an open-ended veto or revenue franchise over network construction.

The FCC’s August 7, 2026 Federal Register notice identifies the practical problem. It proposes that all authorizations needed for a particular wireline deployment in a particular right-of-way generally be acted on within 120 days from the first required application, because sequential approvals can stretch for months or years and make planned builds uneconomic. It also proposes limiting fees to actual and direct right-of-way management costs. INCOMPAS, in September 2026 comments, argues that delays, above-cost fees, and burdensome conditions are exactly the barriers Section 253 was designed to prevent.

A default of “local control unless proven blocking” sounds modest, but it assigns the wrong risk. Fiber projects depend on crews, financing, make-ready coordination, construction windows, and customer commitments. If a provider must litigate every delayed permit or excessive fee one municipality at a time, the deterrent effect arises before any tribunal reaches the merits. Small and competitive providers are least able to absorb that uncertainty, so the default protects incumbency more than local democracy.

The strongest counterargument is serious. Counties and cities, including the National Association of Counties in its 2026 advocacy materials, warn that preemption may underfund permit offices, weaken inspection, and compromise safe management of streets and sidewalks. Local officials know pavement conditions, congestion, drainage, emergency access, and neighborhood disruption better than federal regulators. A blunt deemed-granted rule could reward sloppy applications and overload small jurisdictions.

That concern should shape the remedy, not defeat the default. The rule should require published fee schedules, prompt written incompleteness notices, tolling for applicant failures, extensions for complex projects, and preserved enforcement of neutral safety, traffic-control, restoration, bonding, and inspection rules. But after the deadline expires, or after a fee exceeds documented direct cost, the burden should shift to the locality. Preemption should be presumptive, targeted, and limited to the offending delay, charge, or condition.

The conclusion-changing evidence would be a strong record showing that most delayed or high-fee approvals reflect applicant defects or unavoidable engineering conflicts rather than local leverage or administrative drift. On the current record, the better default is federal preemption of presumptively prohibitive delays and above-cost charges, while preserving local control for transparent, neutral, safety-related right-of-way management.
rationale: The answer is based on current primary materials from the FCC’s August 2026 Federal Register notice and Section 253 of the Communications Act, plus contemporaneous stakeholder positions from INCOMPAS and the National Association of Counties. It states a clear default, addresses the strongest counterargument, identifies uncertainty that could change the conclusion, and the word-counting capability confirmed answerBody is within range.
